note: HUMAN-GROUNDED positional corpus. Every entry exists because a reputable human source
explicitly named the concept for this position — never because an engine liked a move.
The division of labour is the point, and it is recorded per entry:
the CONCEPT and its explanation come from the human annotation;
Stockfish verifies only whether the annotated move is sound, what it prefers,
and whether the positional claim survives concrete calculation.
engine.agrees is therefore a FINDING, not a filter. An annotated move the engine
does not choose is kept, because the concept can be sound while the move is not,
and that distinction is exactly what a learner needs and what an engine-labelled
corpus destroys.
fen_verified records how the position was obtained. 'replay' means the whole game
was played through the page's own move generator, so the FEN is derived rather than
transcribed. Two game scores from reputable sources have already failed that check.

alternate_concepts_considered was originally one list, and the stress test showed why that was wrong: it lumped concepts that are ALSO TRUE but secondary together with concepts that would be WRONG here. Reporting the first is correct behaviour and reporting the second is a false positive, so they are now separate fields and only rejected_as_wrong counts against the system.

fen_concept_realised exists for entries where the concept only appears after a FORCED reply. 9.Nxc6 creates a doubled isolated pawn, and it does so after Black recaptures; asking about the position between the two halves of the exchange is asking before the concept exists.

concept_role is scored, not decorative. tools/corpus_check.py measures a positive example by whether the concept is reported, a NEGATIVE one by whether it is NOT, and an ambiguous one by whether it is present without being required to lead. An earlier version of that checker had one rule for all three, which scores a negative example as a success exactly when the system has failed it.

Two positions carry more than one entry, deliberately. Adams-Kasparov after 21...Kxh7 is a NEGATIVE example for king-attack and an AMBIGUOUS one for king-safety, because the two claims about that position have opposite answers: the black king really is exposed, and there really is no attack. Splitting them is the only way to test both.

move_after_uci exists for the same reason fen_concept_realised does, one step further on: some concepts are realised by a FORCED REPLY that is a move rather than a position. Capablanca-Mattison 1929 is the case - 15.Ng5 does not change the count of pieces bearing on the black king by one, and 15...f5 permanently removes a shield pawn.

rejected_as_wrong is the sharpest test in this file and it is the easiest field to get wrong. It must list only concepts whose application here would be FALSE - never ones that are merely secondary, and never ones a naive reader might over-weight. Three entries in this corpus were drafted with a true concept in that list (space, trapped-piece, pawn-break), and each one manufactured a false positive out of correct output. When the checker reports a rejected alternate, the first question is whether the alternate is actually wrong.

`side` names the colour a NEGATIVE entry is about, and it exists because the sharpest negatives are per-side. Nimzowitsch's blockading bishop on d4 must not be called bad in a position where Black's bishop on d7 correctly is, and a side-agnostic list cannot state that. It required carrying `subjects` through to the API's concepts_all, which had never been exposed there.

Two entries added 2026-09-02 give weak-square its first human grounding, and both are NEGATIVE, which is the right way round for a concept whose own record says every pawn move creates squares no pawn can guard. Both come from one article by a named grandmaster who built the positions as traps for exactly the reading a mechanical detector performs; the second names no side, because the claim is that NEITHER side can use the square.

`attributed_by` names the PERSON whose claim the entry rests on, and it is the field the validation ladder reads - not `annotator`, which is prose and can say things like 'unattributed training page' while still looking like grounding. Backfilled across the file on 2026-09-02, at which point exactly one entry turned out to have no person behind it (karpov-kasparov-1985-g16), and it now correctly grants its concept no human-grounded rung. This is the second time a rung in this project was found counting something looser than its own definition, and both times the number went down.

One entry, added 2026-09-02, is scored on CONFIDENCE rather than on presence, and is the first of its kind here: Ftacnik-Roiz 2009, where White really does have the two bishops and a grandmaster's note reads 'please note how idle White's bishops are' in a position Stockfish scores at -2.66 for him. Nothing the system says is false, so `bishop-pair` does not belong in rejected_as_wrong; what is wrong is the weight. The entry's `confidence` is the annotator's, the checker compares it with the system's, and the gap is a recorded failure rather than a guard fitted to one position.

Torre-Karpov 1977 is the first human-grounded negative for `space`, and it is worth reading beside the two weak-square negatives: all three are positions a named author BUILT to catch the reading a mechanical detector performs, and in all three the raw Layer 3 feature is present and loud. That is what makes them live tests rather than vacuous ones - nine controlled squares to zero, ten holes including d5, a permanent hole on d5 in the Sveshnikov - and in each case what stops the report is a condition the concept's own record already stated.

concept_roles.positive: the concept clearly applies, on the annotator's authority
concept_roles.negative: the board superficially resembles the concept and it should NOT be labelled that way
concept_roles.ambiguous: the concept contributes but is not clearly the primary explanation

positions.annotator: Nicholas Van Der Nat (Chess.com), following the classical literature
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 77 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator
positions.human_annotation: 'The critical moment comes at move 9 when Rubinstein plays 9.Nxc6!, trading the knight to give Black a doubled, isolated c-pawn. Black now has two problems: a weak d-pawn AND a weak c-pawn.'
positions.explanation: The concept applies because the capture MANUFACTURES the second weakness rather than exploiting an existing one. Before it Black has one target, the isolated d5 pawn; after it Black has two, on c6 and d5, and they cannot both be defended by pawns. This base's own detector confirms the structural claim: after 9...bxc6 Black's pawns stand on a, c, c, d, f, g, h with three islands.

engine.agrees: substantially — the annotated move is the engine's second choice, 0.05 behind its first
engine.note: The engine marginally prefers 9.Nb5. A five-hundredth of a pawn is not a disagreement about the plan, and the structural consequence the annotator describes is not in doubt.

positions.why_not_alternates: doubled-pawns and the isolated pawn are the RESULT and are recorded separately; what makes this two-weaknesses is that a second, separated target is created on purpose. piece-exchanges describes the mechanism, not the aim.
positions.fen_after_note: The position the annotated move reaches. A move-based concept describes what the move ACHIEVES, so the checker looks here as well as at the position before it.
positions.fen_concept_realised_note: After 9.Nxc6 bxc6, the forced recapture. The doubled isolated c-pawn the annotation is about exists only here.

positions.human_annotation: 'After patient maneuvering, Rubinstein plays the instructive 20.e3! This seemingly small move accomplishes a great deal: it gains a tempo by attacking Black's queen, opens a diagonal for the bishop, and clears the second rank so the rook can swing from f2 to c2, doubling on the c-file.'
positions.explanation: A quiet move whose entire purpose is to improve the pieces that are doing least — the f1 bishop, shut in, and the f2 rook, off the file that matters. The concept's condition is satisfied exactly: nothing urgent is happening, so the right move is the one that improves the worst-placed piece.

engine.agrees: yes — the annotated move is the engine's first choice
engine.note: A rare clean agreement between a century-old annotation and a modern engine on a quiet move.

positions.why_not_alternates: semi-open-file names where the rook is going and not why this move is right. prophylaxis was rejected: nothing of Black's is being prevented, White's own pieces are being improved, which is the distinction the two records exist to keep apart.
positions.fen_after_note: The position the annotated move reaches. A move-based concept describes what the move ACHIEVES, so the checker looks here as well as at the position before it.

positions.human_annotation: 'Now Rubinstein plays 24.b4!, the decisive pawn break. The immediate threat is 25.b5, attacking the immobilized c-pawn a third time. Black is forced to play 24...a6, creating yet another weakness: the a6-pawn.'
positions.explanation: The human claim is that the pawn break forces a THIRD target into existence on a6, stretching a defence already tied to c6 and d5. The concept is well attested here; the MOVE is not the engine's.

engine.agrees: NO — the engine plays 22.Rb2 at +4.24 and does not rank the annotated move in its top three, all of which are at most +1.52
engine.note: Recorded as a disagreement rather than resolved. The strategic idea the annotation describes is real and the game bears it out, and the engine sees a much stronger continuation that the annotator does not mention. Both are true. This is why concept_role here is AMBIGUOUS: the concept contributes and is not the whole explanation of why the position is winning.

positions.why_not_alternates: minority-attack was considered and rejected — this is not a Carlsbad structure and White is not advancing a minority into a majority. pawn-breaks describes the move; two-weaknesses describes its purpose.
positions.fen_after_note: The position the annotated move reaches. A move-based concept describes what the move ACHIEVES, so the checker looks here as well as at the position before it.

positions.annotator: lichess study following the standard literature; corroborated by a Chess.com retrospective; NAMED: Nagesh Havanur (ChessBase, 2022) and Anthony Levin (Chess.com, 2022)
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 81 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator
positions.human_annotation: 'We've reached a position with hanging pawns. Usually, the side with hanging pawns should place his pieces actively and try to advance the pawns at an appropriate moment. Here, however, Spassky's pieces are passively placed.' NAMED SOURCES ADDED 2026-09-02, after the validation ladder was tightened to require a person rather than a page: Anthony Levin names the structure outright - 'Fischer began to pressure what would become hanging pawns on c5 and d5' - and Nagesh Havanur's notes to the same game speak throughout of White's 'pressure on the hanging pawns', including on the parent game Furman-Geller, Moscow 1970, where Timman and Andersson are cited for '17.Ba4! Qb6 18.Ne5 followed by 19.Rfd1 with pressure on the hanging pawns'.
positions.explanation: The structure is present by definition — c5 and d5 abreast with no b- or e-pawn — and the annotation is careful to say the structure alone is not the problem. The concept applies here in its NEGATIVE aspect because the precondition for the good version, active pieces, is absent. This base's detector independently reports c5 and d5 as pawns no pawn can defend on files the opponent has none.

engine.best_move: (not searched: the annotated claim is about the STRUCTURE, not this move)
engine.agrees: not applicable — the annotation names a structure, not a best move
engine.note: Deliberately not engine-scored. The human claim here is 'this is a hanging-pawns position and Black's pieces are passive', which is a description rather than a move recommendation, and running a search would answer a question nobody asked.

positions.why_not_alternates: isolated-queen-pawn is explicitly WRONG here and is the reason this entry exists: two hanging pawns defend the squares in front of one another and an isolani has nobody to do that, so assessing them as an isolated pawn misreads the structure.

positions.annotator: lichess study following the standard literature; corroborated by a Chess.com retrospective; NAMED: Nagesh Havanur (ChessBase, 2022) and Anthony Levin (Chess.com, 2022)
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 81 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator
positions.human_annotation: 'Fischer proceeds to bust open the position... 20.e4! d4 21.f4 Qe7 22.e5! - fixing the pawns on dark squares to emphasize the power of the light-squared bishop in a more open position.' The Chess.com retrospective adds that 20...d4? 'opened the c4-square for the light-squared bishop, left a weak pawn on e6'. NAMED SOURCES ADDED 2026-09-02: Havanur, '20.e4! probing Black's pawn centre at its most vulnerable point.' Levin, 'After Fischer struck in the center with 20.e4!, Black's most clear positional error in the game occurred: 20...d4?.'
positions.explanation: The break's purpose is not material but to FORCE one of the hanging pawns to commit, which is the standard method against that structure. Re-pointed from pawn-breakthrough to pawn-break after the stress test: this base had no concept for a structural break at all, only the sacrificial motif for forcing a passer, and the annotated position exposed the gap.

engine.agrees: yes — the annotated move is the engine's first choice at +0.40
engine.note: Fischer's break is confirmed as objectively best, fifty years later.

positions.why_not_alternates: pawn-breakthrough is explicitly wrong: nothing is sacrificed and no passer is forced through. minority-attack requires a Carlsbad structure and a pawn minority advancing; neither is present.

positions.annotator: lichess study following the standard literature; corroborated by a Chess.com retrospective; NAMED: Nagesh Havanur (ChessBase, 2022)
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 81 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator
positions.human_annotation: '30.h4! Restricting the knight on h7 even further.' NAMED SOURCE ADDED 2026-09-02: Havanur, '30.h4! After this move neither the black queen nor the knight can use g5 as a springboard.' - which is the restraint claim stated by a named annotator, where the entry had rested on an unattributed study.
positions.explanation: A pawn move whose only purpose is to take squares from an enemy piece — g5 and f6 for the knight on h7 — rather than to attack anything. That is restraint as this base distinguishes it from prophylaxis: no specific plan is being prevented, the opponent's general mobility is being reduced.

engine.agrees: partially — the annotated move is the engine's THIRD choice at +3.75, against +4.15 for 30.e6
engine.note: The engine prefers pushing the passed pawn at once. Fischer's move is 0.40 behind and wins as played. Recorded as partial agreement: the restraining idea is real and there was a faster route, which is a normal thing for a fifty-year-old annotation to have missed and not a reason to drop the concept.

positions.why_not_alternates: prophylaxis was considered and rejected on this base's own distinction: prophylaxis prevents a specific enemy idea, restraint reduces general mobility. Black has no concrete plan here to prevent.

positions.annotator: Mikhail Botvinnik, annotating his own game (tr. Douglas Griffin)
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 116 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator, from a database score that matches every move the annotation names
positions.fen_after_note: The position 20...Qc7 reaches. White's knight has no square: 21.Nxa5 b6 traps it, so it has to go to c5 where it does not stand safely, and that is the constraint the annotation is about.
positions.human_annotation: '20...Qc7! The turning point of the game - the initiative now passes to Black. Since 21.Nxa5 b6 22.Nb3 Qxc3 is by no means in White's favour, the knight has to be placed on c5, where it does not stand safely.'
positions.explanation: This is the concept in its defining form and it is why the entry exists. Botvinnik does not claim Black is better; he claims the roles have swapped - from here White answers and Black asks. The move itself does nothing visible: it steps off the b-file, eyes c3, and leaves White's knight on b3 with no good square, so every White move for the next several is a reply. The concept record's own test is met exactly: 'one side is making threats the other must answer' and 'the answering side has no time for a plan of their own'. The record's warning is met too - the initiative is not detectable from this position as a static feature, which is why this base has no detector for it and this entry is human ground truth rather than a matcher test.

engine.agrees: on the move, completely - 20...Qc7 is the engine's first choice at depth 22, ahead of 20...O-O by 0.15. On the assessment, not at all: the engine still gives White about half a pawn from Black's side of the board.
engine.note: That split is the finding, and it is worth more than agreement would have been. Holding the initiative is not the same as standing better, which is exactly what the concept record says and exactly what an engine-labelled corpus would have destroyed by throwing this position away.

positions.why_not_alternates: tempo is the unit the initiative is spent in, not the concept here; the annotation is about who is answering whom. two-weaknesses is the slow method the concept record records as being in direct tension with the initiative, and reading this move that way would give the reader the opposite instruction about how fast to play.

positions.annotator: Raymond Keene (GM), The Spectator Australia
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 61 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator
positions.human_annotation: '27...Qe5. Capablanca is really doing his upmost on the fourth rank with his strongest piece, but the queen is no match for White's heavily centralised knights and rooks. Black had to try an exchange sacrifice and play 27...Rxe3!'
positions.explanation: The surface of an initiative is all here and none of the substance, which is what makes it a negative example. From move 20 Capablanca's queen has been to c4, c5, h5 and now e5, hitting something every time, and White has answered every time - Rxd6, Rad1, Ne3, Nd4, Nc4. Count only 'one side keeps making threats and the other keeps answering' and Black has the initiative. The concept record's actual test fails: every one of White's forced replies also CENTRALISES a piece, so the answering side is improving while it answers. The record states this directly as a false-positive trap: 'a series of checks is not an initiative. If the opponent's forced replies improve their position, you are helping them.' This is that trap in a world-championship-class game.

engine.agrees: on both halves, and independently. The engine's first choice at depth 22 is 27...Rxe3, which is the move Keene says Black had to try, and the game move 27...Qe5 is second and 0.36 worse. Black is lost either way, which is the point: the side with the 'threats' is two pawns down in evaluation.
engine.note: A rare case of a 2017 GM annotation and a 2026 engine naming the same move for the same reason.

positions.why_not_alternates: piece-activity is TRUE here and is the right label - an active queen is exactly what Black has. Calling it an initiative upgrades activity into a claim about who controls the game, which is the specific error the concept record warns against.

positions.annotator: Jon Speelman (GM), reproduced by ChessBase; the king-safety sentence is quoted from a community annotation and is corroborated, not relied on
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 52 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator
positions.fen_after_note: The position the recapture reaches, and the one both annotators are judging: Black's king stands on h7 with no pawn cover at all, White's rooks are doubled on the g- and h-files, the h-pawn is on h5 and the bishop is on g5.
positions.human_annotation: 'Black sees no threats following either gxf7 or gxh7. His king may look exposed, but in actuality, there is no immediate danger to his king, and Garry knows that his attack is much stronger at the moment. ... If 22.h6, ...g6, and Black's defenses hold. The king cannot be driven from h7, even with a rook sacrifice on g6.' Speelman, on the same position: 22.Be3 was the best response for White, and Adams instead, 'seeing no good way to continue his attack, panicked and blundered'.
positions.explanation: Every mechanical sign of a winning king attack is present - opposite-side castling, a pawn storm that has arrived, the shield gone, two rooks on the files pointing at the king, a bishop on g5 and a queen able to reach h6 - and the attack does not exist. This is the sharpest kind of negative example because nothing about the pattern is missing; what is missing is a threat, and a threat is a property of the position's concrete lines rather than of its shape. Black mates first on the other wing (22...Nxc2 and 26...Qa3, with ...Rxb2+ behind it). Any detector that reports a king attack from attacker counts and a broken shield will report one here.

engine.agrees: fully, and it agrees with the named human move. Searching the position AFTER 21...Kxh7, Stockfish 18 at depth 22 returns Be3 - the move Speelman names as White's best - and scores it at -2.13 from White's side. The side with the 'attack' is two pawns worse.
engine.note: Searched from White's move rather than Black's, because the claim being tested is about the position the recapture reaches, not about whether the recapture was forced.

positions.why_not_alternates: pawn-storm is TRUE and should be reported: White really did play g4-g5-h4-h5-g6. What must not be inferred from it is an attack. greek-gift would be flatly wrong - nothing was sacrificed on h7, a pawn arrived there with check and was taken.

positions.annotator: Jon Speelman (GM), reproduced by ChessBase; the king-safety sentence is quoted from a community annotation and is corroborated, not relied on
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 52 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator
positions.fen_after_note: Speelman's recommendation, which the engine also returns. Note what it is: White defends b2 and abandons the attack. Even the best move here treats the exposure of BLACK's king as irrelevant.
positions.human_annotation: Speelman: 22.Be3 was the best response for White; Adams, 'seeing no good way to continue his attack, panicked and blundered' with 22.Nb3. The community annotation states the judgement plainly: 'His king may look exposed, but in actuality, there is no immediate danger to his king.'
positions.explanation: This is the same position as the negative entry above and a DIFFERENT claim about it, which is why both exist. King safety genuinely applies: Black's king has no pawn shield, stands on an open h-file with two enemy rooks on it, and that is a real and correctly-observed feature. What it is not is the thing that decides the game - the concept contributes and does not decide, which is the definition of an ambiguous example in this corpus. The concept record already registers the distinction as a false-positive trap: 'an exposed king is not automatically losing.' A system that reports Black's king as exposed here is right; one that concludes Black is in trouble is wrong, and the gap between those two sentences is what this entry measures.

engine.agrees: yes - Speelman's 22.Be3 is the engine's first choice, 0.58 ahead of 22.Bf4. The evaluation of -2.13 is the measure of how little the exposed king is worth to the side attacking it.
engine.note: Same search as the negative entry; recorded on both because the two entries make different claims about one position.

positions.why_not_alternates: king-attack is the concept that would be WRONG here and is recorded separately as a negative example. luft is a different idea about a different rank and does not describe a king already outside its shelter.

positions.annotator: Nicholas Van Der Nat (FM), following Irving Chernev's Logical Chess: Move by Move
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 49 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator
positions.fen_concept_realised_note: After the forced 15...f5. The permanent weakening the annotation is about exists only here - before Black replies, the shield is still intact.
positions.human_annotation: Chernev calls 15.Ng5 'a master stroke'. The annotation gives its real purposes: 'The surface threat is 16.Qxh7 mate, but the real purposes run deeper: first, it forces Black to play ...f5, permanently weakening the kingside pawn cover; second, it vacates f3 for the dark-squared bishop.'
positions.explanation: The concept applies in its constructive form: the move is played FOR the damage to the shield, not for the mate threat that forces it. The concept record puts the pawn shield first among the five things that decide king safety and says the shield is 'strongest unmoved, because an unmoved shield presents no target'. After 15...f5 Black's f-pawn has left f7 for good, e6 and the a2-g8 diagonal are permanently softer, and no later move can undo it. The tactical threat is the mechanism; the king-safety damage is the point, and a reading that reports only 'mate threat on h7' describes the smaller half.

engine.agrees: fully - 15.Ng5 is the engine's first choice at depth 22 and 0.66 ahead of the second, and its principal variation begins 15...g6, a different shield concession from the one played, which supports rather than weakens the claim that the move's purpose is the shield.

positions.why_not_alternates: hanging-piece is what this base's tactical layer currently reports for this move, because Qxh7 is winnable material; it is true and it is the least interesting true thing about the move. king-attack is premature: White has not yet committed anything to an attack and the game is won on the queenside diagonal.
positions.move_after_note: Black's forced reply. The concept is realised by this move, not by 15.Ng5: the knight arriving on g5 blocks the bishop that was already looking at h6, so the count of pieces bearing on the black king's zone is 2 before the move and 2 after it. What changes the king's safety is the pawn leaving f7.

positions.annotator: Raymond Keene (GM), The Spectator Australia
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 61 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator
positions.fen_after_note: The move Keene says Capablanca should have played. The game went 18...N6d7 instead, and the difference between the two is the whole content of this entry.
positions.human_annotation: '18...N6d7. It is a mystery why Capablanca did not play the obvious 18...Ne6, fighting more directly for control of the centre.'
positions.explanation: A human annotator naming central control as the criterion that decides between two knight moves, in the game that is the canonical demonstration of the hypermodern claim about the centre. Both candidate moves develop a knight and neither occupies a central square; what separates them is how much they contest d4 and c5 - the concept record's first false-positive trap is exactly this distinction, that 'counting pawns on central squares measures occupation, not control'. The knight on e6 bears on d4 and c5 and holds the tension; the knight on d7 does not, and White's centre rolls forward with 19.Qd2 and 20.Bxd4.

engine.agrees: fully, and it is the strongest confirmation in this corpus. The engine's first choice at depth 22 is 18...Ne6 at +0.80 for Black; the second and third are +0.41 and +0.31; and the move Capablanca actually played, 18...N6d7, is not in the top three at all. A GM's one-line positional judgement about the centre, written in 2017, picks the move a 2026 engine puts nearly half a pawn clear.
engine.note: Searched from Black's side. The 0.39 gap between the recommendation and the runner-up is large for a quiet middlegame move.

positions.why_not_alternates: space is TRUE for White here - the pawns on b5, c4 and d4 are advanced - and an earlier version of this entry listed it as an alternate the annotator rejected, which manufactured a false positive out of a correct report. What would be wrong is outpost: e6 is not protected by a black pawn and is not unassailable, and the whole content of the annotation is that the knight is going there to contest squares rather than to sit on one.
positions.limitation: This base's centralSquareControl() reports center-control for BOTH 18...Ne6 and the game's 18...N6d7, so it does not do the discriminating work the annotation does. Measured: on pawns and minor pieces, Ne6 is +1 and N6d7 is also +1, because moving the f6 knight unblocks the g7 bishop onto d4 and e5. The count cannot tell 'contesting the squares White wants' from 'attacking two other central squares'. Recorded rather than fixed, because tuning the measure until it separates these two particular moves is how a detector stops meaning anything.

positions.annotator: Raymond Keene (GM), The Spectator Australia
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 61 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator
positions.fen_after_note: Capablanca occupies the centre with a pawn. Reti never does, and wins.
positions.human_annotation: Reti, in Masters of the Chessboard, on the system he is playing here: 'The move directs pressure against the centre, prevents 1...e5, and keeps open almost all the possibilities for the first player.' A reader of the game on chessgames.com states the same point about its finish: 'All of Reti's pieces which once controlled the center from a distance now directly occupy the center.'
positions.explanation: This is the position the hypermodern argument is about, and it is an ambiguous example on purpose. After 8.d3 White has not one pawn on a central square; his influence over d4, e4 and e5 comes from a fianchettoed bishop on the long diagonal, a knight on f3 and pawns on c4 and d3. Black is about to occupy the centre with ...e5. Both sides have a coherent claim to be fighting for the centre, and the engine says the position is level - so central control is genuinely present, genuinely the subject of the position, and does not by itself decide anything. Any system that measures central control by counting central pawns would report Black ahead here and the game's own author disagreeing.

engine.agrees: on the assessment, which is the claim being tested. Depth 22 gives -0.23 for Black across all three of its top moves, so neither the distant control nor the coming occupation is worth anything measurable yet. The move recorded here is the game's 9...e5, played a move later; it is recorded for what it shows about occupation, not as a recommendation.
engine.note: The move field is the plan Black carries out, not a move the engine was asked to rank in this position.

positions.why_not_alternates: space is the concept that would be wrong to lead with: White's pawns on c4 and b4 do gain queenside space, and reporting that as the story of this position gets the game exactly backwards. hypermodern-school is the historical label, not a property of the board.

positions.annotator: Nicholas Van Der Nat (FM)
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 87 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator, from a database score; the blog's own printed move orders are not trusted in this project and were not used
positions.fen_after_note: The pawn is now on d4: further advanced, more space, and permanently unsupportable by another pawn. The bargain is struck here.
positions.human_annotation: 'Rubinstein, one of the greatest players never to be world champion, voluntarily accepts an isolated queen pawn, confident that its central control is worth the long-term weakness.' Gelfand states the same division in general terms: 'you have to use your advantage before it disappears. Obviously, this is all about dynamic advantages. With static advantages, the urgency is often much less.'
positions.explanation: The isolated queen's pawn is the textbook case of the classification and this is a game in which the classification decides the result. What Black holds is dynamic - space, an advanced pawn, open lines for the pieces - and it expires as pieces come off. What White holds is static: a fixed target that cannot be repaired, which grows more valuable with every exchange. The concept record's instruction follows directly and the game obeys it: Capablanca trades queens at move 22 and rooks after, and the pawn is still sitting on d4, untouched, when Rubinstein resigns. The record's own false-positive trap applies here too - the classification is not a property of the feature alone, and the same pawn is dynamic on move 15 and static on move 30.

engine.agrees: partly, and the disagreement is informative. The engine's first choice at depth 22 is 15...Qf6 (+0.09 for Black) and the game move 15...d4 is not in its top three. The position is level either way, so the engine is not calling the advance a mistake - it is declining to spend the tension. The annotation's claim is about which KIND of advantage Black is buying, not about whether this was the best move to buy it with, and this base does not let an engine overrule the first because it disagreed about the second.
engine.note: This is the second entry in this corpus where a sound concept sits on a move the engine does not choose, and both are kept for the same reason.

positions.annotator: Nicholas Van Der Nat (FM)
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 87 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator, from a database score; the blog's own printed move orders are not trusted in this project and were not used
positions.fen_concept_realised_note: After 22...bxc6 23.Re7. This is where the transformation has actually happened: the target is gone, Black's pawns are united, and White has the seventh rank instead. Asking about the position between the two halves is asking before the trade is complete.
positions.human_annotation: 'Here it is: 22.Qxc6, trading the queens. At first glance this looks like a mistake, because after 22...bxc6 Black's pawns are united and his once-isolated pawn is no longer isolated at all. Capablanca has apparently thrown away the very weakness he spent the game building an attack against. But this is not a mistake, it is a transformation. In return for giving up the target, he plays 23.Re7 and seizes the seventh rank.'
positions.explanation: A transforming move gives something up, and that is precisely what makes it hard to recognise and easy to mislabel. Twenty moves of pressure on d4 are abandoned in one move; the reader who is following the plan sees a concession. The concept record names this as its first false-positive trap in reverse - 'a transforming move often looks like a concession and can be reported as an error by anything judging moves on what they give up rather than what they get.' What is bought is the seventh rank, and the record's requirement that the new advantage be MORE convertible is met concretely rather than by assertion: the rook on e7 wins a pawn on b6, then another, then produces a passed b-pawn, and the d4 pawn the whole game was about is never captured at all.

engine.agrees: fully. 22.Qxc6 is the engine's first choice at depth 22 (+0.34), ahead of 22.Bb4 (+0.09) and 22.Re2 (+0.05), and its principal variation continues 22...bxc6 23.Kf1 - it likes the resulting ending for the same structural reason the annotation gives.
engine.note: A quarter-pawn gap is small in absolute terms and decisive in kind: the two runners-up are moves that keep the attack on d4, and the engine puts the move that abandons it first.

engine.agrees: fully and by a wide margin. 16.Bf3 is the engine's first choice at depth 22 at +2.48, with the second-best move at +1.64 - a gap of 0.84 in a position with no capture and no check on the board.

positions.fen_verified: replay: all 61 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator

positions.players: Rene Letelier Martner - Robert James Fischer
positions.annotator: WGM Raluca Sgircea and IM Renier Castellanos
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 46 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator
positions.human_annotation: 'His opponent decided to launch an early pawn storm against Black's King's Indian and delay his development. When central pawns are not supported by pieces, they can become an easy target for the opposite side. This is exactly what happened in the game; Fischer didn't wait for his opponent to develop his pieces and immediately started attacking the center.' And the general statement: 'Occupying the center only with the pawns, without developing the pieces or without having coordinated them is known as over-extension and can become a target for our opponent instead of an advantage.'
positions.explanation: The position the literature uses to teach that the centre can be a target, and this base measures White's central control at seven attacks to two, leading on three of the four squares. Both readings are correct and that is the point of an ambiguous entry: the measurement is right, and the verdict everybody attaches to it is wrong. The engine calls the position level. Sixteen moves later Fischer is playing 23...Qxf4+ and White has resigned. The concept record already registers this as its second false-positive trap - 'a big pawn centre is not automatically an advantage; whether it is an asset or a target is a question of timing and support, and that cannot be read off the structure' - and this entry is that sentence given a board. It is also why the matcher's wording states the counts as counts and ends 'ask what kind of centre is on the board before you choose a plan' rather than announcing an advantage.

engine.agrees: on the assessment, which is the whole claim: at depth 22 the position is level, -0.09 from Black's side, with White holding pawns on d4, e5, c4 and f4 and Black holding no central square at all. The game's 7...c5 is the engine's second choice, 0.17 behind 7...dxe5.

positions.annotator: Garry Kasparov on what the sacrifice is; John Watson reporting Petrosian's own account of choosing it

positions.human_annotation: Kasparov: 'Petrosian introduced the exchange sacrifice for the sake of quality of position, where the time factor, which is so important in the play of Alekhine and Tal, plays hardly any role. By sacrificing the exchange just like that, for certain long term advantages, in positions with disrupted material balance, he discovered latent resources that few were capable of seeing and properly evaluating.' On this position: 'Black must stop White's pawns, so Petrosian gives up the exchange at a spot of his own choosing, freeing e7 for the transfer of his knight to d5. Of course, Black gets good compensation for the exchange: his knight is much stronger on d5, as is his bishop, which no longer has an opponent.' positions.explanation: The most famous positional exchange sacrifice ever played, and an AMBIGUOUS example rather than a positive one for a precise reason: after the dust settles White really is the exchange up, this base really does report a material imbalance, and it decides nothing. What decides is the d5 square, which no white pawn can attack and no white bishop can contest once the light-squared bishop has been traded for the rook. The concept applies, it is reported, and a reader who stops there has the position exactly backwards - which is why the entry names WHITE as the side holding the imbalance and asks that nothing be concluded from it.

engine.agrees: completely, and it plays out the plan. 25...Re6 is the engine's first choice at depth 24, 0.76 clear of the second, and its principal variation is 26.Rg3 Ne7 27.Bxe6 fxe6 28.Rf1 Nd5 - the knight reaching d5 by the exact route the annotation describes. Black is still a pawn worse at -1.01, which is the honest part: the sacrifice rescues a difficult position rather than winning one.
engine.note: A 1953 exchange sacrifice for 'quality of position', chosen by a player who said it was too simple to doubt, is a 2026 engine's first choice by three quarters of a pawn.

positions.why_not_alternates: exchange-sacrifice and positional-sacrifice are what the MOVE is and are recorded on their own records from this position. outpost is what the sacrifice buys and does not exist yet - d5 is not occupied for three more moves. positions.annotator: Irving Chernev, quoted; Max Euwe on the ending

positions.human_annotation: 'Here is the move that gives the game its name, 52...Qd5, and Chernev marks it with an exclamation and one word: Blockade. She sits directly in front of White's d-pawn, stopping it dead, and at the same time she eyes weak pawns on both wings. That is the three directions at once: one square, three jobs.' The same page is candid about the position: it 'is objectively a draw with accurate play', and the great annotators disagreed about the cleanest winning path.
positions.explanation: A queen blockading, praised by name, in a position that is objectively drawn - which makes it ambiguous twice over. This base's blockade record carries a false-positive trap that reads almost as a warning against this exact move: 'a piece standing in front of a pawn is not necessarily blockading it usefully. The test is whether the piece keeps its powers there - a queen on a blockading square is doing a knight's chore.' Chernev's point is that here she does keep them: from d5 she stops the d-pawn AND attacks pawns on both wings, which is precisely why the chore is not a chore. The concept applies, the detector reports it, and neither settles whether the position is won.

engine.agrees: with the annotation's own caveat rather than with its enthusiasm, which is the useful outcome. At depth 24 the position is 0.00 and so is 52...Qd5, the engine's second choice among three moves it scores identically. Capablanca won it anyway, and the page says in as many words that the ending is a theoretical draw.
engine.note: An annotation that names its own limits is worth more than one that does not, and this entry is here partly to record that.

positions.why_not_alternates: king-activation is true of both kings and says nothing about the move. passed-pawn would be wrong: White's d-pawn is not passed - Black's e6 pawn stands on an adjacent file ahead of it - which is why this is a blockade of an ADVANCING pawn, the half of the record's precondition that a first version of the detector ignored.

engine.agrees: the position is dead level at depth 24, which is the point: nothing is being won here, least of all a queen.

positions.annotator: Rudolf Spielmann on what a sacrifice IS; Irving Chernev on this move
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 49 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator
positions.human_annotation: Chernev calls the finish 'a queen sacrifice followed by a smothered mate'. Spielmann, classifying sacrifices: 'A sham (temporary) sacrifice involves no risk. After a series of forced moves, the player either recovers the invested material with advantage, or else even mates his opponent. The consequences of the sacrifice were foreseen from the first. Properly speaking, there is no sacrifice, only an advantageous business deal.' A mating sacrifice is one of his three sham types.
positions.explanation: Two named authorities disagree about whether this is a sacrifice, and both are right about different questions - which is exactly what an ambiguous entry is for. By this base's definition, taken from the repository's own SEE test, material that can be taken is offered and the concept applies: seven points of it. By Spielmann's classification the move is a mating sacrifice, sham, and 'properly speaking, there is no sacrifice'. The distinction turns on whether the consequences were calculable, and Stockfish settles that half: mate in two. This base reports the material fact, carries Spielmann's taxonomy on the record since this position exposed that it did not, and does not adjudicate.

engine.agrees: completely, and it decides the half of the question that can be decided: 24.Qg8+ is the engine's first choice at depth 20 and it is MATE IN TWO. A forced mate is precisely Spielmann's condition for a sham sacrifice - the consequences were foreseen from the first.
engine.note: Recorded with mate rather than a centipawn score, because a centipawn score here would be a worse answer than the one available.

positions.annotator: Jan Markos (GM), 'The Winning Academy 32: The Hole', ChessBase, 22 April 2024
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 52 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator, from the pgnmentor score. The diagram Markos gives is 'Black to move', and the move he quotes as played from it (20...Qa6) is the 40th ply of that replay, which is what fixes the position.
positions.human_annotation: "This is one of my favourite positions to test new pupils. Is Black worse, equal, or better? Many club players answer automatically: White is obviously better, look at the hole on d5! In addition, Black has got the 'bad' bishop. In fact, the opposite is true: Black is better. Why? Firstly, and most importantly, the b3-knight is very far from the d5-square. Two squares diagonally are the well-known 'long-short distance' for a knight. It takes four moves for him to travel it, even on an empty board... In the game, Fischer played 20...Qa6 and with energic play proved that Black truly is better."
positions.explanation:
The first human-grounded evidence in this corpus for weak-square, and it is a negative, which is the right way round: the concept's own record says every pawn move creates squares no pawn can guard, so the whole question is which of them matter. d5 IS a hole in Black's camp by every structural test - Black's c-pawn is gone and the e-pawn is on e5, so no black pawn can ever attack it - and Layer 3 reports it as such: holesFor(w) contains d5. What must not be said is that this is White's asset. Markos designed the position as a trap for exactly the reading a mechanical detector performs.

This base is silent, and it is worth being precise about WHICH guard does the work, because it is not the one this session added. The matcher requires a hole a minor piece can reach in ONE move, and White's only minor piece is the knight on b3, four moves away. Markos's reason is finer than the machine's - he counts the knight's long-short distance and notes that White's f-pawn is already on f5, so it is the e4 pawn and the white king that are weak - and the machine's reason happens to agree with it here. That is a pass, not a proof, and the entry records the difference rather than claiming the system reasons as Markos does.

The position is also a live instance of this record's THIRD false-positive trap, 'a weak square only a queen can occupy is usually not a weakness, since cheaper pieces evict her': White's queen is standing on d5 as the diagram is drawn, and is driven off it within six moves.
positions.why_not_alternates: material-imbalance is correctly reported and is exactly what Markos discusses - White's knight against Black's 'bad' bishop, level on points. blockade is correctly reported: White's queen does stand in front of the d6 pawn. What must not be said is that White has a weak square to use.

engine.agrees: on the evaluation, not on the move. Scores are from the side to move, and Black is to move: +0.39 says Black is the better side, which is Markos's whole claim and the opposite of what the hole on d5 suggests. The move Markos quotes as played, 20...Qa6, measures 0.00 and is not in the top three - Fischer's 21...Rc8 next move IS the engine's first choice here.
engine.note: What is being tested is not the move. It is whether a hole in Black's camp may be reported as White's asset, and the engine is here only to say that the side with the hole is the better side. The gap between +0.39 and 0.00 is a fact about 20...Qa6 and is recorded rather than smoothed over; Markos's claim about the SQUARE stands either way.

positions.annotator: Jan Markos (GM), 'The Winning Academy 32: The Hole', ChessBase, 22 April 2024
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 65 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator, from the pgnmentor score. The diagram is 'Black to move' and the continuation Markos quotes - 20...d5! 21.cxd5 Rb6! - is plies 40-43 of that replay, which is what fixes the position.
positions.human_annotation: "Again, the d5-hole truly resembles a keyhole with no fitting key. White's knight seems to be better placed than in the previous examples, on an empty board its travel to d5 would only take two moves. However, Black succeeded in constructing an interesting cage: his b4 and f4 pawns guard all the roads to d5. Perhaps White would like to put a bishop to d5. But this is impossible as well. Therefore, d5 is a 'no man's land'. Neither side can make any use of it."
positions.explanation:
The sharper of the two, and it names NO side, because Markos's claim is that neither side can use the square. A per-side negative would be the weaker statement.

Everything superficial points the other way. This is the Sveshnikov, the opening whose entire reputation is the d5 hole; Black's structure has the hole permanently (no c-pawn, pawn committed to e5); Layer 3 reports ten holes for White including d5; and a knight sits on c2, two moves from the square. A detector built on 'no friendly pawn can ever attack it' says d5 and says it loudly.

What makes it a no man's land is that the roads in are closed by two black pawns that a structural scan reads as WEAKNESSES: b4 and f4 are both undefendable by any black pawn, and this base's own two-weaknesses matcher lists f4 among the things Black should be worried about. Markos calls the same two pawns a cage. Both readings are mechanically defensible from the pawn skeleton alone and only one of them is true of this position, which is the clearest statement in this corpus of what a structural feature cannot decide.

The entry is kept as a weak-square negative rather than a two-weaknesses negative because Markos does not discuss the principle of two weaknesses, and putting a concept in rejected_as_wrong on an annotator's behalf is how three earlier entries in this file manufactured false positives. What the f4 disagreement is, is a limitation recorded on the two-weaknesses record.

After 20...d5 the square ceases to exist, which is Kramnik's point in playing it - so fen_after tests the same claim in its easiest form, and the position before the move is the one that carries the entry.
positions.why_not_alternates: bishop-pair and doubled-pawns are correctly reported for Black and are both true. The doubled f-pawns are the Sveshnikov's own bargain and Markos's 'cage' is made of one of them. What must not be said is that d5 is a square either side can use.

engine.agrees: on both counts, and unusually cleanly. Scores are from the side to move: 0.00 for Black, which is Markos's 'Black is equal', and the move he quotes - 20...d5! - is the engine's first choice, settled from depth 8, with the second best a third of a pawn worse.
engine.note: The engine says nothing about whether d5 is a weak square and was not asked to. It says the position is level and that abolishing the square is best play, which is what makes 'no man's land' a claim about the board rather than about taste.

positions.annotator: Jan Markos (GM), 'The Winning Academy 6: Hypnotised by the bishops', ChessBase, 2 March 2022
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 56 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator. The score was taken from a contemporary Polish-notation report of the round and matches Markos's quoted continuation move for move - 14.gxf3 0-0 15.Rd1 Qe7 16.Na4 Ba7 17.Bh3 Rad8 18.Nb2 d4 - which is what identifies the game rather than the header.
positions.human_annotation: On the decision that produced this position: "With his last move 12...Bg4, Roiz created the threat of Bxf3, blowing up the shelter of White's king. However, Ftacnik was not impressed. Instead of carefully parrying the threat with e.g. 13.Be2, he decided for the active 13.Bf5??, assuming that he is in a win-win situation. Either Black exchanges the bishops, and then White is closer to an endgame with a clear plan against the isolated d5-pawn, or he takes on f3 and then White will enjoy the bishop-pair. However, White's thinking was too one-dimensional. In fact, the f3-knight is an important piece that protects crucial central squares. Also, after the exchange on f3 the white king will be extremely weak, and his army stuck in the centre will not be able to come to help him." And on this position: "The final attack against the weakened White's kingside has just begun. Please note how idle White's bishops are, and how nicely the black cavalry controls the centre." The article's thesis: "we tend to overestimate what is well-defined and clear-cut, and underestimate what is vague and hazy... we tend to overestimate it compared to hazier assets as 'initiative' or 'cooperation of pieces'."
positions.explanation:
RECORDED FAILURE, and the first entry in this corpus scored on CONFIDENCE rather than on presence.

White does have the two bishops and Black does not. Nothing this base says about the position is false: it reports the pair, the doubled f-pawns, Black's isolated d-pawn, Black's control of the centre. What it cannot do is what Markos's whole article is about - weight them. It reports the pair at MEDIUM confidence, as the second thing in the list, in a position Stockfish scores at -2.66 for the side holding it, and where a grandmaster's note reads 'please note how idle White's bishops are'.

The entry therefore sets the annotator's confidence to LOW and lets tools/corpus_check.py's confidence measure catch the gap, rather than putting `bishop-pair` in rejected_as_wrong. It is not wrong to say White has two bishops. Three earlier entries in this file manufactured false positives out of correct output by listing a true concept as rejected, and the note at the top of this file says so.

What was tried and did not work: the guard added on the same day for this record's third trap - 'a pair where one bishop is shut in by its own pawns is not really a pair' - does not fire here, and should not. White's bishops share their colour with three of six pawns each and see seven and five squares. They are not buried by pawns; they are simply pointing at nothing while the king they left behind is being mated. No static feature in this base separates those two states, and the record says as much in its own second trap: 'half a pawn is an AVERAGE over many games and can be arbitrarily wrong in one position.'

The honest reading is that this is the same class of limit as the recorded piece-activity failure on Reti-Capablanca 1924: the concept is army-level or position-level, the annotation is about what the pieces are DOING, and inventing a guard to make one position score would be fitting a rule to a case.
positions.why_not_alternates: doubled-pawns, isolated-queen-pawn and center-control are all correctly reported and are all part of Markos's account - the shattered kingside, the d-pawn White was playing against, and the black knights that 'nicely control the centre'. None of them is wrong. What is wrong is only the WEIGHT given to the bishop pair beside them.
positions.limitation: The system reports bishop-pair at medium confidence where the annotator's is low. That is a measured confidence overclaim and it is left standing, because the only ways to remove it are to invent a guard that fits this one position or to change the expected answer.

engine.agrees: emphatically, on the evaluation. Scores are from the side to move, and White is to move: -2.66 with the bishop pair in hand and every alternative worse. The game's 19.e4 is also the engine's first choice, so White is not being punished for the move but for the position the bishops were bought with.
engine.note: The engine cannot say whether a bishop pair is worth anything and was not asked to. It is here to establish that the side holding the clear-cut, well-defined asset is losing by more than two and a half pawns, which is what makes this a test of WEIGHTING rather than of detection.

positions.annotator: Raluca Sgircea (WGM) and Renier Castellanos (IM), 'Positional Chess Understanding: The Space Advantage', TheChessWorld, 2015
positions.fen_verified: replay: all 68 plies replayed legally through blind-chess.html's move generator, from the pgnmentor Karpov collection. The position is the one the annotators' note attaches to - 'Qg2 was the only move and continue the waiting game, not weakening any more' is written at White's 26th.
positions.human_annotation: The game is introduced as "a great example of how not to play when you have space advantage. Instead of controlling black's counterplay, white deliberately went on to grab more space and all of a sudden found himself under a very strong counterattack." At this exact position the note reads: "26.Qg2 was the only move and continue the waiting game, not weakening any more." And the article's general warning, which is this base's `space` record's first trap said in other words: "just the fact that one side has more space doesn't necessarily mean that is also better. Sometimes the spatial advantage is confused with over-extension... in the quest for space, one side tends to advance too many pawns, leaving weakness behind or not being able to support this advances with pieces. As a result, the opponent will find counterplay."
positions.explanation:
The first human-grounded negative for `space`, and it is a live test of a guard added the same day rather than a vacuous one.

White's pawns control NINE squares in Black's half against zero: b4, c4, e4, f4, g4 and h5 make as unambiguous a territorial advantage as this corpus contains, and the matcher's own threshold is a gap of two. Until this session it would have reported it, with confidence, in a position Stockfish scores at -3.01 after the move actually played. What stops it now is the record's own first trap - "counting controlled squares is mechanical and over-reports. Space with no entry point wins nothing" - and Layer 3 finds no entry square for White at all: every route in is either covered by a black pawn or loses the piece that takes it.

What this base DOES report is the other side of the annotation. `piece-activity` names BLACK, 24 active moves to 12, which is the counterattack the authors say arrives out of nowhere; and `semi-open-file` names Black's rook on the c-file, which is where the game ends - 34...Nxc4, and White resigned.

The engine agrees with the annotators about the move and not merely about the position: 26.Qg2, the move they call the only one, is Stockfish's first choice at +0.05, and 26.e5, the grab for more space, measures -3.01. A three-pawn swing on one move is what "suddenly found himself under a very strong counterattack" looks like in numbers.

Why `space` is in rejected_as_wrong rather than treated as secondary: this base does not define the concept as territory. Its record defines it as territory that gives the pieces room and denies the opponent room, and states in its first trap that territory with no entry point wins nothing. Reporting it here would not be reporting something true but secondary; it would be reporting the concept as the record defines it, in a position where the record's own exclusion applies.
positions.why_not_alternates: piece-activity for BLACK and semi-open-file for Black are both correctly reported and are both the annotation's own subject - the counterplay White allowed. battery for White is true and harmless. What must not be said is that White's territory is an asset.

engine.agrees: on the move and on the evaluation. Scores are from the side to move, and White is to move: 26.Qg2 - the move the annotators call the only one - is Stockfish's first choice at +0.05, settled from depth 15, and the game's 26.e5 measures -3.01 and is not in the top three. A three-pawn swing on one move.
engine.note: The engine says nothing about whether nine controlled squares are a space advantage and was not asked to. It establishes that the waiting move holds the balance and the grab for more space loses by three pawns, which is what makes 'how not to play when you have space advantage' a claim about the board.
